newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa govt delays oil industry margin decision.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa govt delays oil industry margin decision.

text.p: The South African Cabinet this week failed to make a decision on the long-awaited wholesale margin increase for the oil industry.
The industry's hopes are now pinned on the Cabinet's next meeting on October 23 if it is to get its increase in the November gasoline price adjustment.

Mineral and Energy Affairs director-general Gert Venter told Reuters that Wednesday's meeting had not been "a crucial cut-off date" despite high expectations in the industry that a decision would be made.
He said the Cabinet probably wanted further information or clarity on certain issues, although this did not deny the urgency of some move on the margin.

A spokesman for the Central Energy Fund, which administers gasoline price adjustments, confirmed that it would have to be advised of any margin increase by October 30 if it was to be included in the next price adjustment.
The oil industry has applied for a three cents a litre hike in its wholesale margin, the first rise since September 1993.

South African Petroleum Industry Association (Sapia) director Colin McClelland on Tuesday told the Africa Oil 1996 conference that an increase in the margin had become due on January 1 this year but had not yet been approved.
"We hope for approval of this increase...in the November price adjustment which is due on Wednesday, November 6," he said.

McClelland told Reuters on Thursday that any decision on margins "was not timed out yet...we will have to wait" for the next Cabinet meeting. The industry had hoped to receive the increase by mid-1996.

But it is understood the decision was delayed due to the appointment of a new mineral and energy affairs minister due to a cabinet reshuffle following the National Party's decision to quit government at the end of June.

With the demand for gasoline expected to outstrip national refining capacity within the next year or two, the industry has said that future investment decisions depended on restoring margins and generally providing greater clarity and certainty about the government's future energy policies.
Sources report that a policy "white paper" on energy is being finalised and will hopefully be released late in 1996 or early 1997.
